title: The Table by the Window
author: Lantern Original
summaryTr: Küçük bir istasyon kafesinde geçici olarak çalışan Ada, kasabanın eski yürüyüş yollarını çizen bir marangozla aynı masayı paylaşır. Birlikte hazırladıkları harita, gelecekleri hakkında söylemekten kaçındıkları şeyleri görünür kılar.
paragraphs: On her first morning at the station cafe, Ada put a small sign on the table by the window. It said Reserved. She had not reserved it for a customer. The afternoon light reached that table, and she needed somewhere to draw after the breakfast rush. Her aunt had promised that she could use a corner of the cafe while she worked there for six weeks. Ada planned to earn enough money for the first month of a design course in the city. She had already bought a yellow folder for her application.

At half past nine, a man in a blue work jacket came in, ordered tea, and moved the sign to the next table. He spread several sheets of paper beside the window. Ada watched him from behind the counter. She waited until he took out a pencil, then walked over. 'That table is reserved,' she said. He looked at the sign he had moved. 'It always says that on Tuesdays.' This seemed a strange answer. 'Today is Monday,' Ada replied. He glanced at the calendar on the wall, and it did say Monday.

The man gathered his papers at once. 'Then I have made two mistakes before breakfast.' His smile was small, and Ada tried not to return it. Her aunt Vera came through the kitchen door with a tray of warm rolls. 'You have met Ben,' she said. 'He made the shelves. And repaired the door. And promised to stop taking payment in tea.' Ben lifted his cup. 'This is a separate matter.' Vera explained that he usually drew walking maps at the window. Ada looked at the papers again. They showed streets, trees, and the river.

Ben offered to use another table, but Ada had already noticed a line running through the old school yard. 'You cannot walk there now,' she said. 'The fence is locked.' Ben frowned. He had walked that route himself in the winter. Ada told him that a building company was using the yard. She had passed it on her way from the bus station. He rubbed out the line carefully. 'That is why I need help,' he said. 'People remember a town differently from the way it is.' Ada moved her yellow folder to one side.

The map was for a small walking festival at the end of August. Ben had offered to replace the old map, which sent visitors towards a bridge that no longer existed. He could measure a door, build a cupboard, or make a table stand straight on an uneven floor. Drawing clear directions was harder. His hills looked like piles of bread, and his river was too wide. Ada laughed when he said this, then apologised. 'No, you are right,' he told her. 'Last week somebody asked whether this was a map of an island.'

Ada showed him a simple way to mark a path. She used a broken line for a rough track and a solid one for a paved route. Then she drew a small bench. Ben leaned forward. 'That is exactly the bench outside the library.' It was not meant to be, but she liked that he had recognised something in it. They agreed to share the window table after two each afternoon. Ada would help make the map clear. In return, Ben would build a flat board for her drawings. Neither of them called this an important agreement.

For the next three days, their work stayed polite and ordinary. Ada served soup, washed cups, and counted her tips. Ben arrived with dust on his sleeves and information written on the backs of receipts. A path near the river had six steps, not four. The public garden closed at five on Sundays. The bakery owner would let walkers fill their water bottles. Ada put these details in a neat list. Ben tested the pencils she left on the table and always chose the shortest one. By Thursday she had sharpened it before he arrived.

On Friday they went out to check the longest route. Ada wore new boots because they looked suitable for serious walking. After twenty minutes she wished she had worn her old trainers. Ben did not comment when she slowed down. At the next gate, he stopped to measure its width with a tape from his pocket. 'For people with walking frames or pushchairs,' he explained. Ada sat on a low wall while he wrote the number. When they started again, he took a shorter path without suggesting that she needed it.

At a field above the river, they found that the promised view was hidden behind a thick line of bushes. Ben read the old leaflet aloud. 'Enjoy an open view of the valley.' Ada stood on a stone and saw only leaves. 'Perhaps the valley has gone out for lunch.' He laughed so suddenly that she nearly lost her balance. He offered his hand, and she took it to step down. His palm was warm and rough. Afterward, they both became very interested in deciding whether the field deserved a star on the map.

They ate sandwiches beside a closed boat house. Ben had brought two apples and a small knife. He cut an apple into pieces and placed them on the paper around Ada's sandwich. She told him about the course in the city. It lasted a year and included work on signs, books, and public spaces. 'I want to make things people can actually use,' she said. He nodded towards her notebook. 'You already do.' She explained that helping with one map was different from earning a living. 'Different in size,' he replied. 'Perhaps not in purpose.'

Ben had grown up in the town, left to work with a furniture company, and returned three years earlier. Ada asked whether he had missed home. He considered the question. 'I missed having enough time to finish things properly.' At the company, he had built the same kitchen twenty times. At home, customers brought him difficult cupboards, broken chairs, and ideas that were almost possible. The work was less certain, but it belonged to him. Ada liked this answer. He did not make staying sound brave or leaving sound foolish. They were simply different choices.

At the cafe that evening, Vera looked at the red marks on Ada's heels and gave her a bowl of warm water. 'Was the walk useful?' she asked. Ada described the narrow gate, the hidden view, and the boat house. Her aunt listened with an expression that became more cheerful after each detail. 'And Ben?' Ada looked down at her feet. 'He knows where all the paths go.' Vera passed her a towel. 'That was not quite what I asked.' Ada dried one foot slowly and changed the subject to the price of tomatoes.

The following Monday, Ada found her drawing board against the window. Ben had made it from a smooth piece of pale wood. There was a narrow edge at the bottom to stop pencils falling off, and a handle cut into the side. On the back, he had written her name in small, careful letters. She ran her finger across the wood. It was much better than the simple board she had expected. When he arrived, she said thank you twice. He looked pleased by the first thank you and embarrassed by the second.

That afternoon, the festival organiser visited. Mrs Hale wanted the map finished in twelve days. A local printer had offered a lower price if all the pages arrived together. She liked Ada's drawings, especially the little station building. Then she pointed at an empty corner. 'Could you add the summer house at Mill Garden?' Ben put down his pencil. The garden had been closed for years. Mrs Hale said its new owner might open it during the festival. A picture would encourage him. Ada thought this sounded like drawing a promise that nobody had made.

Ben agreed. 'We should ask him first.' Mrs Hale waved one hand. 'Of course. But the old map includes it.' After she left, Ada found the summer house on a faded page. It was a pretty wooden building beside the river. Ben had repaired its roof when he was sixteen. His father had taken him there during a school holiday and trusted him with tools he had never used before. 'Is your father still working?' Ada asked. Ben shook his head. 'He died four years ago.' She waited, allowing him to decide whether to say more.

He said his father had known every small building along the river. They had often argued about work. His father preferred careful repairs; Ben had wanted to make everything new. 'Now I hear myself telling customers exactly what he used to say.' Ada smiled. Her mother did the same thing with recipes. There was a quiet moment between them, full of things neither needed to explain. Then Ben opened his notebook. They would visit the owner of Mill Garden on Wednesday. Ada wrote the appointment beneath a drawing of two people sitting on a bench.

The owner, Mr Finch, met them at a tall green gate. He was not unfriendly, but he was busy and did not want visitors near his house. Ben explained that the public path could reach the summer house without passing the windows. Ada showed him a possible route. Mr Finch studied it, then pointed towards the river. 'The bottom steps are broken. I cannot invite people to fall into the water.' They walked down together. Three wooden steps had become soft, and a rail moved when Ben touched it. The problem was clear enough.

Ben said he could price the repairs. Mr Finch answered that he had no spare money for a building he rarely used. Ada began putting the map away. Then she noticed an old sign under a bush. It said River Walk, with an arrow towards the summer house. 'Was this once part of the path?' Mr Finch said it had been, long before he bought the property. Ada did not argue that it should become public again. Instead, she asked whether he would consider opening it for one day if the festival paid for safe steps.

On their way back, Ben said she had asked the right question. 'You made it possible for him to say yes without giving up his garden.' Ada felt pleased, though she tried to sound practical. They still had no money and only nine days. Ben could provide some wood left from another job, but it would not be enough. Ada suggested asking the festival committee to pay the rest. He shook his head before she finished. 'Their budget is already tight.' She stopped walking. 'You do not know the answer until you ask.'

Ben looked towards the station. 'People here already help me.' Ada could hear the change in his voice. He did not want to talk about it. She could have left the subject alone, but she was tired and wanted him to see her point. 'Helping is not a debt you can never pay back.' He said he knew that. His face suggested he did not. They reached the cafe without solving anything. He collected his bag and went straight to his workshop. For the first time, Ada left the shortest pencil unsharpened on the table.

That night she wrote the first page of her course application. It asked for an example of a design problem and how she had solved it. She described the map, then stopped at the sentence about working with another person. Had she actually listened to Ben? He knew the town's money problems better than she did. But knowing a difficulty was not the same as accepting it forever. She crossed out several sentences. In the end, she wrote that good directions had to make sense to people who did not already know the way.

Ben came early the next morning. He stood by the counter while Ada filled the sugar bowls. 'I was short with you yesterday,' he said. She put down the packet. 'I pushed too hard.' He explained that after his father died, neighbours had kept the workshop open by bringing him small jobs. Some had paid more than the work was worth. He was grateful, but he worried that every request reminded them of that time. Ada had not known this. 'We can ask the committee together,' she said. 'For the festival, not for you.'

They made a proper plan with the cost of wood, screws, and Ben's time. Ada insisted that his time belonged on the page. He agreed, although he used a smaller number than she expected. Mrs Hale took the plan to the committee. By the afternoon, they had enough money for materials and half the work. Ben could donate the remaining hours if he wanted. That choice mattered to him. He shook Ada's hand in a serious way when she brought the news. She laughed, and he kept her hand just a little longer than necessary.

On Saturday, Ada helped carry wood through Mill Garden. Mr Finch had marked the route with pieces of white cloth so they would not damage his plants. Ben removed the broken steps while Ada pulled old screws from the sound boards. She had expected to be useless, but he gave her real tasks and showed her how to do them. At noon, Mr Finch appeared with lemonade. He watched the work for a while, then fetched a chair and began cleaning the old sign. By late afternoon, all three of them had paint on their clothes.

When Mr Finch went inside, Ada and Ben sat in the summer house. The river moved slowly below them. Through a gap in the trees, they could see trains entering the station. Ada said that from here the town looked like something she had once imagined. Ben asked what she meant. 'A place where I might belong without having to become smaller.' He did not answer quickly. Then he said, 'I hope it can be that.' His knee touched hers beneath the narrow bench. Neither moved away, though there was plenty of room.

He walked her home after they had cleaned the brushes. Outside Vera's gate, he asked whether she would like to have dinner with him. Ada looked down at her trousers. 'Without paint?' Ben smiled. 'We can try.' They chose the following Thursday because he had a delivery on Wednesday and she worked late on Tuesday. It was a very ordinary conversation about times and places. Yet after he left, Ada stood at the gate for almost a minute. She had not expected an ordinary conversation to change the appearance of the whole street.

On Monday, an email arrived from the design college. Ada had been invited to an interview. The message included a practical task: bring three examples of work and explain one in detail. The interview was in the city on Thursday afternoon. She read the date twice. Travel would take three hours each way, and the last train home arrived after ten. She began writing to Ben, deleted the message, and started again. Before she could send it, Mrs Hale entered with three new corrections to the map. Ada put her phone under the counter.

The corrections took most of the afternoon. A cafe had changed its opening hours. A path was going to close for repairs. Somebody wanted the car park shown larger than the church. Ben was working outside town and could not help. By the time Ada called him, she had made the interview into a much bigger problem in her mind. 'Thursday is difficult,' she said. He asked if she wanted another day. She heard disappointment where there may only have been a question. 'I have to go to the city.' There was a short pause.

'For the course?' he asked. Ada said yes. 'That is good news.' His voice was careful. She explained that she had not been accepted yet and might not be able to afford everything. 'But you want to go,' he said. She did. He suggested dinner on Friday instead. It was the right suggestion, but Ada felt strangely sad after the call. Until that moment, her future and her time with Ben had existed in separate rooms. Now somebody had opened a door between them, and she did not know how the rooms fitted together.

On Thursday, Ada carried her drawing board onto the early train. She had chosen the walking map, a set of food labels, and a book cover she had made for practice. At the college, the other visitors seemed younger and more confident. One had a huge black case with silver corners. Ada held her wooden board against her knees. When the interviewer asked about it, she explained that a friend had made it. Then she began describing the map. She spoke about clear paths, honest information, and the difference between a beautiful view and a useful route.

The interviewer asked what had been hardest. Ada could have said the short deadline or the changing information. Instead, she described Mill Garden and the conversation with Ben about asking for money. 'The drawing was the easy part,' she said. 'I had to understand what different people were worried about.' The interviewer nodded and asked another question. Ada stopped comparing herself with the other visitors. She knew this work. She had stood beside the broken steps, held the old sign, and checked every narrow gate. She could explain why each line belonged on the page.

When she returned, Ben was waiting outside the station with a paper bag. 'Vera said you might have missed dinner.' Inside were two rolls and an apple. Ada wanted to hug him, but she was suddenly shy. They sat on the wall by the bicycle stands. She told him about the interview, including the large black case. He listened without interrupting. When she finished, he said he thought they would offer her a place. 'Do you want them to?' she asked. Ben looked at the tracks. 'I want you to have the choice.'

Their dinner on Friday was at a small restaurant above a shop. The windows were open, and someone in the square below was practising the trumpet badly. Ada ordered too quickly and received a dish with much more pepper than she expected. Ben exchanged plates with her without making a joke. They talked about brothers, favourite films, and the terrible rooms they had rented in other towns. For an hour, the map and the course disappeared. Ben told a story about carrying a wardrobe up the wrong stairs. Ada laughed until the waiter smiled at them.

After dinner, they walked towards the river. Ben stopped beside the closed market. 'I like being with you,' he said. There was no clever speech around it. Ada was grateful for that. She told him she liked being with him too. He asked whether he could kiss her, and she said yes. The kiss was brief and a little awkward because they both smiled halfway through. Then a bicycle bell rang behind them, and they stepped out of the path. Ada took his hand. They walked on slowly, with the river beside them and no immediate need to speak.

The next morning, the college offered Ada a place. She was washing a large soup pot when her phone rang, so Vera held it near her ear. Ada said thank you several times and promised to confirm by Tuesday. Her aunt hugged her, leaving a wet mark on the back of her shirt. For a few minutes, everything was simple. Then Ada opened the list of costs again. The course fee was covered by her savings, but rent and travel would use almost everything she could earn. There was no comfortable space for mistakes.

Ben found her with a calculator at the window table. He congratulated her, then sat opposite without reaching for a pencil. Ada said she was considering waiting another year. 'Because of the money?' he asked. 'Mostly.' He noticed the last word. She looked at the map between them. 'I have only just found something good here.' Ben was quiet. She wanted him to say that staying would be enough. She also knew she might hate him later if he did. At last he said, 'I would miss you. That is true. It is not a plan for your life.'

Ada knew he meant to be fair, but the words hurt. 'You sound as if you have already decided it cannot work.' He shook his head. 'I do not know how it would work.' She asked whether he wanted to find out. Before he could answer, a group of cyclists entered and ordered lunch. Ada stood up too fast, knocking a pencil onto the floor. Ben picked it up. When she returned, he had gone to the workshop, leaving a note that said they needed to check the final map before four. It was painfully sensible.

They checked the map that afternoon with Mrs Hale sitting between them. Ada found two spelling mistakes. Ben corrected the number of steps at Mill Garden. They approved the final page and watched Mrs Hale send it to the printer. Everyone should have been pleased. Instead, Ada felt as if they had finished something she was not ready to lose. Ben said he had work to do. She said she understood. Both statements were true, but they left out the important part. Vera watched them leave through different doors and wisely said nothing.

On Sunday, Ada went to the summer house alone. The new steps were firm, and Mr Finch had planted flowers beside the entrance. She sat on the bench and opened her notebook. Instead of drawing, she made two lists: what she knew and what she feared. She knew she wanted the course. She knew she liked Ben. She feared being forgotten in the city and becoming unhappy if she stayed. The fears were not facts. Writing them separately did not solve everything, but it made the page less frightening. There was room between the two lists.

Ben arrived carrying a small tin of paint. He looked surprised to see her. 'The sign needs one more coat,' he explained. Ada closed her notebook, then opened it again. 'I think I asked you to promise something neither of us can promise.' He sat down at the other end of the bench. 'I think I hid behind being reasonable.' She showed him the lists. He read them carefully. Then he added one sentence under what she knew: The city has trains. Ada laughed despite herself. 'That is not a complete answer.' 'No,' he said. 'But it is a beginning.'

They talked for nearly an hour. Ben could visit on some weekends, but not all. Ada would have busy periods when she needed to work. Neither wanted the other to spend money they did not have. They agreed to try for three months and then talk honestly about how they felt. It was not the kind of promise Ada had seen in films. It was smaller, with dates and train fares inside it. Yet it felt stronger than pretending distance would not matter. Ben moved closer. This time, when their knees touched, Ada leaned against his shoulder.

On Tuesday, she accepted the college place and paid the deposit. After pressing the button, she felt both excited and sick. Ben sent a message with a drawing of a train. It was a terrible drawing, with wheels of different sizes. She saved it anyway. That afternoon, she found a room in a shared flat near the college. The owner agreed to a video call and showed her the kitchen, the desk, and the view of a brick wall. Ada booked a visit before signing anything. She was learning that hope worked better when she checked the details.

The printed maps arrived on Thursday. Ada opened the first box with a bread knife while Ben held the cardboard steady. The colours were clear. The river curved gently across the page, and the station cafe stood in one corner. On the back, Mrs Hale had included their names. Ada had not expected that. Ben turned the sheet over twice. 'It looks like a real thing,' he said. She understood exactly what he meant. All the afternoons of small choices had become something a stranger could fold, carry, and use to find a way through town.

On the morning of the festival, rain hit the cafe windows before breakfast. Mrs Hale arrived in a large waterproof coat and said the riverside route might need to close. Ben went out to check it while Ada helped Vera make extra soup. At ten, he returned with wet hair and mud on his boots. The lower path was flooded in two places. The summer house could still be reached from the upper lane. Ada took a thick blue pen and marked a temporary route on a large copy of the map. Then she made smaller notices for the gates.

They expected people to complain, but most were glad to know where they could walk safely. A father thanked Ada for showing the steps clearly because his little daughter tired easily. Two older women chose the shorter route and returned with wet shoes and cheerful faces. At noon, the rain stopped. Mr Finch opened the summer house and put a pot of tea on the table. Ben called to say that people were using the new steps. Ada looked around the crowded cafe. Their map had changed, but its purpose had survived. It still helped people find their way.

Late in the afternoon, Vera took over the counter so Ada could visit Mill Garden. She followed the temporary signs and found Ben speaking to a boy who wanted to know how bridges stayed up. Mr Finch had brought out another table. Walkers stood under the trees, sharing biscuits and comparing routes. Ada saw one of their maps sticking out of a woman's pocket, soft at the corners from use. Ben came towards her. 'You missed the largest crowd.' She shook her head. She had not missed what she had come to see. The place was open, and people were there.

Her last week passed quickly. She trained a new cafe assistant, packed her clothes, and visited the city room with Vera. The brick wall outside the window was real, but so were the clean kitchen and the friendly woman who would share the flat. Ben helped carry a small desk from Vera's attic. He repaired one loose leg and refused to paint over the old scratches because Ada liked them. They spent her final evening eating soup at the window table. For once, neither had brought work. The short pencil rested in a jar beside the till.

At the station the next morning, Ben carried her drawing board while she pulled a heavy suitcase. The train was already waiting. Ada felt a sudden wish to make the goodbye either very grand or very quick. Instead, she put her arms around him and stayed there for a moment. They had chosen the date of his first visit. They had checked the price of the ticket. They would still miss each other. Ben handed her the board. 'Call when you arrive,' he said. She kissed him, stepped onto the train, and found a seat by the window.

Three weeks later, Ben visited the city. Ada met him outside the station and gave him a folded sheet of paper. It was a small map showing the way to her flat, a cheap place for dinner, and a park where they could sit if the weather stayed dry. Near the station, she had drawn a slightly uneven train. Ben recognised his own picture and laughed. 'You should have used a better designer.' Ada took his bag with one hand and his hand with the other. 'I liked this one,' she said. Then they followed the first line together.

quiz.q: Why is Ada working at her aunt's cafe?
options: To buy the cafe
To earn money before a design course
To learn to cook professionally
To replace the festival organiser
quiz.explainTr: Ada tasarım kursunun ilk ayındaki giderleri karşılamak için para biriktirir.

quiz.q: Why does Mr Finch first refuse to open the summer house?
options: The wooden steps are unsafe
He dislikes the map's colours
The garden has no entrance
He is selling the property
quiz.explainTr: Alt basamaklar çürüktür ve korkuluk gevşektir; ziyaretçilerin düşmesinden endişelenir.

quiz.q: What makes asking the committee for money difficult for Ben?
options: He has already spent its money
He wants to cancel the festival
He feels neighbours have already helped him a lot
He does not know any committee members
quiz.explainTr: Babasının ölümünden sonra komşuları ona iş vererek destek olmuştur; yeniden yardım istemek onu rahatsız eder.

quiz.q: What do Ada and Ben decide about her move?
options: Ben will close his workshop immediately
Ada will refuse the course
They will stop seeing each other
They will try the relationship and talk again after three months
quiz.explainTr: Uzak mesafeli ilişkiyi üç ay denemeye ve ardından dürüstçe değerlendirmeye karar verirler.

quiz.q: What does Ada give Ben when he visits the city?
options: A new set of tools
A map with places they can visit together
A ticket back to the town
The key to the summer house
quiz.explainTr: Ada dairesini, uygun fiyatlı bir yemek yerini ve parkı gösteren bir harita hazırlar.
